headline: 38 Pounds on an Eel at 3 A.M. — The Gut Is Waking Back Up
subhead: Current's rebuilding out of the neap and the big bass are back on the current seams after dark, right on schedule.
body_markdown:
Two-forty in the morning, chest waders locked to my belt, standing on the rocks at Plum Gut with a 14-inch black eel threaded on a 9/0 hook. Second cast into the meat of the rip, I feel the take — not a tap, a lean, like the current itself grabbed the rod. Ninety seconds later I'm walking a 38-pound bass up onto the rocks in the dark, gills flaring, water still ripping past my knees at better than three knots. That's the fish that tells you everything you need to know about this week.

We called this one. Said last week the current-dependent spots were soft off the neap cycle and would come back to life as the moon built toward full — and that's exactly what's happening. The Race and Plum Gut both went quiet the back half of last week, current so lazy you could practically wade across the seam without getting swept. Now with the moon filling out toward August, the tide's rebuilding fast, and the fish know it before we do. By Thursday night the ebb through the Gut was running with real authority again, and that's when the eel bite turned on.

Daytime, forget it — surface temps are sitting in the low 70s from New London out to Fishers Island, and these bass have gone nocturnal on us just like everywhere else in the Sound right now. I'm not wasting daylight hours chucking bucktails into open water hoping for a miracle. The program is night tide, dark water, current seams. Eels on the drift through the Gut on the last two hours of the ebb, or bunker chunks fished dead-still on the bottom in 30 to 50 feet where the current stacks bait against the rock piles off Orient Point. Fresh bunker, not the frozen stuff — cut it thick, let it soak on a fish-finder rig with just enough weight to hold bottom, and wait. The bites aren't subtle. When a 40-class fish eats a chunk in that current, your rod tip doesn't tap, it disappears.

Bluefish are the daytime show, and they're not shy about it. Bunker schools are getting pushed hard through The Race and around the Fishers Island side, and the blues are riding them like they own the place — which right now, they do. I've had double-digit blue days on 2-ounce Kastmasters and green machines, fished fast on the retrieat right through the boiling bait. If you see gulls working tight and diving, don't idle over — get on it, because these schools don't sit still for long with this much current moving through. Expect that blitz pattern to keep spreading, same as it has been coast-wide, so don't be surprised if it pushes harder into western Sound territory over the next week while we keep getting our share out here too.

Porgies are the one thing out here I don't have to qualify. The classic rock piles — Bartlett's Reef, the humps off Fishers Island, the rubble bottom inside Plum Gut itself — are stacked. Small hooks, squid strips or sandworms, just enough sinker to hold in the current, and you can fill a five-gallon bucket in an hour on the right stage of tide. This fishery doesn't care about moon phase or thermal gradients, it just eats. Good one to fall back on with the kids or when the striper bite makes you want to put your head through a rock.

Fluke are tougher right now, and I won't dress it up. The open, flat-bottom drifts that produced in June have gone quiet as the water's warmed — summer flounder don't like sitting in 71-degree water on a mud flat any more than I'd like sitting in a sauna. They've pushed into the inlet-adjacent structure, the deeper bends and current edges around Plum Gut and the Orient Point rip where it stays cooler and keeps moving. Bucktail-and-Gulp combo, half-ounce to an ounce depending on drift speed, white or chartreuse, dragged slow right on the edge where the fast water meets the slower eddy. You'll mark fish on the machine stacked right on that seam. Weakfish have shown flickers of life in the same zones but nothing consistent enough to plan a trip around — a fish here, a fish there, mostly incidental on the fluke gear.

Looking ahead, the current's only going to keep building as we run toward the full moon in early August, and that's good news across the board for anything that depends on moving water — bass, blues, fluke, all of it. My money for the next week is on the same program: dark-water eel and chunk bites at Plum Gut and The Race on the back half of the ebb, bluefish wherever the bunker gets pinned against structure, porgies as the reliable afternoon fallback. If the wind stays out of the south and light like it has been, I'd be on the rocks again well before sunrise — that 38-pound fish didn't come easy, but it came right on time with the tide, and that's the whole game out here.
